title: Latency vs Throughput: Why Fast Means Two Things
sources: AlgoMaster, 'Latency vs Throughput': latency is the time a single request takes from start to finish (measured in milliseconds); throughput is how many requests a system handles per unit of time (e.g. requests per second)

Volt Active Data, 'Latency vs Throughput: Navigating the Digital Highway': highway analogy - latency is how long one car takes to travel the road, throughput is how many cars pass per unit of time; adding lanes raises throughput without making one car faster
DesignGurus, 'Difference between throughput, latency and concurrency': low latency and high throughput are separate goals; a system can be good at one and poor at the other

lines.text: When people say an app is fast,
they could mean two completely different things.
Latency is how long one car takes
to get from the start to the finish.
Throughput is how many cars arrive every minute.
In apps, latency is the wait after you tap,
and throughput is how many requests
add more lanes, and way more cars get through,
but each car still drives just as long.
short waits, and lots of traffic.
Tomorrow: one bigger computer, or more computers?
